Physiology-01.question: ১) Which of the following contribute to the platue phase of the action potential of ventricular muscle fibers-?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Ca²⁺ influx. The plateau phase (Phase 2) of the ventricular muscle action potential is mainly due to:

  • Opening of slow L-type calcium channels

  • Influx of Ca²⁺ into the cardiac myocyte

  • Balanced by a reduced outward K⁺ current

This prolonged calcium entry helps maintain contraction and prevents tetany of cardiac muscle.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Na⁺ influx – Responsible for the rapid depolarization phase (Phase 0) of ventricular action potential.

  • K⁺ influx – Not a major contributor to cardiac action potential phases.

  • K⁺ efflux – Responsible mainly for repolarization (Phase 3).

High-yield points:

Ventricular action potential phases:

Phase Main ion movement
Phase 0 (Depolarization) Na⁺ influx
Phase 1 Initial K⁺ efflux
Phase 2 (Plateau) Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels)
Phase 3 (Repolarization) K⁺ efflux
Phase 4 Resting membrane potential

Exam pearl:
Cardiac plateau phase = L-type Ca²⁺ channel opening.

Physiology-01.question: ২) Which part of the ECG corresponds to ventricular repolarization?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is T wave. The T wave represents ventricular repolarization on the ECG.

ECG components:

  • P wave → Atrial depolarization

  • QRS complex → Ventricular depolarization

  • T wave → Ventricular repolarization

  • PR interval → Time for impulse conduction from atria to ventricles (AV node and His-Purkinje system)

High-yield points:

ECG component Represents
P wave Atrial depolarization
QRS complex Ventricular depolarization
T wave Ventricular repolarization
PR interval AV conduction time

Exam pearl:
T wave = ventricular repolarization.

Physiology-01.question: ৩) Cardiac cycle is the term used to describe the sequence of events that occur as the heart works to pump blood through the body. The opening of the atrioventricular(AV) valves occurs at about the same time in the cardiac cycle as-
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is end of isovolumic contraction.

During the cardiac cycle:

  1. Ventricular systole begins

    • AV valves close → produces first heart sound (S1)

    • Isovolumic contraction phase starts (all valves closed)

  2. Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure

    • AV valves remain closed

  3. End of isovolumic contraction

    • Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure

    • AV valves open

    • Ventricular filling begins

The other options are incorrect:

  • Beginning of diastole – AV valve opening occurs near the beginning of ventricular diastole, but the precise event is after isovolumic relaxation, not simply at the start.

  • Beginning of systole – AV valves close at the beginning of systole, not open.

  • First heart sound – Due to closure of AV valves, not opening.

High-yield points:

Cardiac cycle:

  • AV valve closure → S1 → beginning of systole

  • Aortic/pulmonary valve opening → ventricular ejection

  • Semilunar valve closure → S2 → beginning of diastole

  • AV valve opening → ventricular filling

Exam pearl:
AV valves open after isovolumic contraction, when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.

Physiology-01.question: ৪) Myocardial contractility is best correlated with the intracellular concentration of?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Ca²⁺. Myocardial contractility is directly related to the intracellular calcium concentration.

Mechanism:

  • Action potential → Ca²⁺ enters cardiac myocytes through L-type calcium channels

  • Ca²⁺ triggers further Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

  • Ca²⁺ binds to troponin C

  • Actin–myosin interaction increases → myocardial contraction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Na⁺ – Important for rapid depolarization (Phase 0), but not the main determinant of contractility.

  • K⁺ – Important for repolarization and resting membrane potential.

  • Cl⁻ – Has minimal role in myocardial contraction.

High-yield points:

Cardiac contractility depends on:

  • Intracellular Ca²⁺ availability

  • Calcium entry through L-type channels

  • Calcium-induced calcium release

Exam pearl:
↑ Intracellular Ca²⁺ → ↑ myocardial contractility (positive inotropy).

Physiology-01.question: ৫) At which site is systolic blood pressure the highest?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is aorta. The highest systolic blood pressure is found in the aorta because it receives blood directly from the left ventricle during ventricular systole.

Approximate pressures:

  • Aorta: ~120 mmHg systolic

  • Renal artery: slightly lower than aortic pressure

  • Pulmonary artery: ~25 mmHg systolic

  • Central vein: ~0–5 mmHg

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Central vein – Has the lowest pressure in the circulation.

  • Pulmonary artery – Carries deoxygenated blood but is a low-pressure system.

  • Renal artery – Receives systemic arterial pressure but lower than the aorta due to vascular resistance.

High-yield points:

Systemic circulation pressure:

  • Highest → Aorta

  • Lowest → Central veins/right atrium

Exam pearl:
Maximum systolic pressure in cardiovascular system = Aorta.

Physiology-01.question: ৬) After massive blood transfusion in a patient, which of the following abnormality will occur?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is metabolic alkalosis. After massive blood transfusion, citrate used as an anticoagulant in stored blood is metabolized by the liver into bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), causing an increase in plasma bicarbonate and resulting in metabolic alkalosis.

Other contributing factors:

  • Citrate binds calcium → hypocalcaemia (during rapid transfusion)

  • Citrate metabolism → ↑ bicarbonate production

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Metabolic acidosis – May occur in shock or poor tissue perfusion, but is not the typical acid-base abnormality from transfusion itself.

  • Respiratory acidosis – Due to hypoventilation, not related to transfusion.

  • Respiratory alkalosis – Due to hyperventilation, not the classic transfusion complication.

High-yield points:

Massive transfusion complications:

  • Metabolic alkalosis → citrate metabolism → ↑ HCO₃⁻

  • Hypocalcaemia → citrate binding Ca²⁺

  • Hyperkalaemia → stored blood potassium

  • Hypothermia

  • Dilutional coagulopathy

Exam pearl:
Massive blood transfusion → citrate → bicarbonate → metabolic alkalosis.

Physiology-01.question: ৭) Which dietary component is needed for synthesis of DNA and influence the production of RBCs?
Physiology-01.exp:
The dietary component required for DNA synthesis and influencing RBC production is folic acid (Vitamin B9).

Mechanism:

  • Folate is required for purine and thymidine synthesis

  • Essential for DNA replication and cell division

  • Rapidly dividing cells such as bone marrow erythroid precursors are highly dependent on folate

Deficiency causes:

  • Megaloblastic anaemia

  • Impaired RBC maturation

  • Hypersegmented neutrophils

High-yield points:

DNA synthesis →

  • Folic acid (B9)

  • Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)

Megaloblastic anaemia causes:

  • Folate deficiency

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency

Exam pearl:
Folate = DNA synthesis + RBC maturation.

Physiology-01.question: ৮) Which of the following condition can stimulate erythropoietin secretion?
Physiology-01.option1: Low level of O2 in blood
Physiology-01.option2: Normal level of hemoglobin in RBCs
Physiology-01.option4: An increased blood flow through kidneys
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is low oxygen level in blood (hypoxia). Erythropoietin (EPO) secretion from the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney is stimulated by reduced oxygen delivery to tissues.

Mechanism:

  • ↓ Blood oxygen content → renal hypoxia

  • Kidney detects hypoxia

  • ↑ Erythropoietin secretion

  • ↑ Bone marrow RBC production

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Normal level of haemoglobin in RBCs – Does not stimulate EPO secretion.

  • High RBC count – Increases oxygen-carrying capacity and suppresses EPO production.

  • Increased blood flow through kidneys – Improves oxygen delivery and reduces EPO secretion.

High-yield points:

Stimulus for erythropoietin:

  • ↓ Tissue oxygenation (hypoxia)

  • Anaemia

  • High altitude

  • Chronic lung disease

Source:

  • Kidney (mainly)

  • Liver (minor, especially fetal life)

Exam pearl:
Renal hypoxia → ↑ EPO → ↑ RBC production.

Physiology-01.question: ৯) What is serum?
Physiology-01.option1: Whole blood sample from which all cells are removed
Physiology-01.option2: Plasma from which fibrinogen and clotting factors are removed.
Physiology-01.option3: The portion of blood that is composed of RBCs
Physiology-01.option4: Plasma from which only albumin and globulins are removed
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is serum. Serum is the liquid portion of blood obtained after clotting, so it is essentially plasma without fibrinogen and most clotting factors.

Process:

  • Blood clots → fibrinogen converted to fibrin

  • Clotting factors are consumed

  • Remaining fluid = serum

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Whole blood sample from which all cells are removed – This describes plasma, not serum.

  • The portion of blood composed of RBCs – This is the cellular fraction/packed red cell component.

  • Plasma from which only albumin and globulins are removed – Incorrect; albumin and globulins remain in serum.

High-yield points:

Component Contains
Plasma Water + proteins + fibrinogen + clotting factors
Serum Plasma − fibrinogen/clotting factors
Whole blood Cells + plasma

Exam pearl:
Serum = Plasma without fibrinogen.

Physiology-01.question: ১০) Site of blood cell production at late fetal life
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is red bone marrow. During late fetal life, the major site of haematopoiesis (blood cell production) becomes the red bone marrow.

Stages of fetal haematopoiesis:

  1. Yolk sac → Early embryonic life (first site)

  2. Liver → Major site during mid-fetal life

  3. Spleen → Contributes during fetal period

  4. Red bone marrow → Main site in late fetal life and after birth

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Yolk sac – Site of primitive blood cell formation in early embryonic life.

  • Liver – Major haematopoietic organ during the middle fetal period.

  • Thymus – Site of T-cell maturation, not general blood cell production.

High-yield points:

Sites of fetal haematopoiesis:

Period Main site
Early embryo Yolk sac
Mid fetal life Liver (± spleen)
Late fetal life Red bone marrow
Adult Red bone marrow (axial skeleton)

Exam pearl:
Late fetal haematopoiesis = red bone marrow.

Physiology-01.question: ১১) Sky rise of ESR is found in
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is multiple myeloma. A sky-high ESR (very markedly elevated ESR, often >100 mm/hr) is classically associated with multiple myeloma due to increased production of monoclonal immunoglobulins.

Mechanism:

  • ↑ Immunoglobulins → ↑ plasma protein concentration

  • Promotes rouleaux formation of RBCs

  • RBCs settle faster → markedly increased ESR

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Polycythaemia vera – Increased RBC mass increases blood viscosity and usually causes a low ESR.

  • Pregnancy – ESR can increase due to increased fibrinogen, but usually not “sky-high.”

  • MI – ESR may rise due to inflammation, but not typically extremely elevated.

High-yield points:

Very high ESR (>100 mm/hr) causes:

  • Multiple myeloma

  • Severe infection

  • Giant cell arteritis

  • Some malignancies

Exam pearl:
Sky-high ESR + rouleaux formation = Multiple myeloma.

Physiology-01.question: ১২) The extrinsic pathway is assessed by...
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is PT. The extrinsic pathway of coagulation is assessed by Prothrombin Time (PT).

PT evaluates:

  • Extrinsic pathway → Factor VII

  • Common pathway → Factors X, V, II, fibrinogen

The other options are incorrect because:

  • BT (Bleeding time) – Assesses platelet function and primary haemostasis.

  • CT (Clotting time) – A nonspecific older test assessing overall coagulation.

  • APTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time) – Assesses the intrinsic pathway (Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII) and common pathway.

High-yield points:

Test Pathway assessed
PT Extrinsic + common pathway
APTT Intrinsic + common pathway
BT Platelet function
Thrombin time Fibrinogen → fibrin conversion

Exam pearl:
Extrinsic pathway = Factor VII = PT.

Physiology-01.question: ১৩) Intrinsic coagulation pathway starts with
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is activation of Factor XII (Hageman factor). The intrinsic coagulation pathway begins when Factor XII is activated after contact with negatively charged surfaces (e.g., exposed collagen).

Sequence:
Factor XII → XI → IX → VIII → X → common pathway

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Activation of Factor VII – Starts the extrinsic pathway.

  • Activation of Factor II (prothrombin) – Occurs in the common pathway to form thrombin.

  • Activation of Factor X – This is the convergence point where intrinsic and extrinsic pathways enter the common pathway.

High-yield points:

Pathway Initiating factor Test
Intrinsic Factor XII APTT
Extrinsic Factor VII PT
Common Factor X → II → I PT & APTT

Exam pearl:
Intrinsic pathway starts with Factor XII activation.

Physiology-01.question: ১৪) Which blood group has no antigen
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is blood group O. In the ABO blood group system, group O red blood cells have neither A nor B antigens on their surface.

ABO antigens:

Blood group RBC antigen
A A antigen
B B antigen
AB A + B antigens
O No A or B antigen

The other options are incorrect because:

  • A – Has A antigen on RBCs.

  • B – Has B antigen on RBCs.

  • AB – Has both A and B antigens.

High-yield points:

ABO system:

  • Universal donor (RBC) → O negative

  • Universal recipient (RBC) → AB positive

Exam pearl:
Blood group O = no A/B antigen on RBC surface.

Physiology-01.question: ১৫) Immature RBC is called
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is reticulocyte. A reticulocyte is an immature red blood cell that has recently lost its nucleus but still contains residual ribosomal RNA.

  • Reticulocytes are released from the bone marrow into circulation.

  • They mature into erythrocytes within about 1–2 days.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Proerythroblast – Earliest nucleated precursor of the erythroid series in bone marrow.

  • Early normoblast – A nucleated erythroid precursor before maturation.

  • Intermediate normoblast – A later nucleated precursor stage.

High-yield points:

Erythropoiesis sequence:

Proerythroblast → Early normoblast → Intermediate normoblast → Late normoblast → Reticulocyte → Mature RBC

Exam pearl:
Immature circulating RBC = Reticulocyte.

Physiology-01.question: ১৬) RMP of Never fiber-
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is −70 mV. The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a nerve fibre is approximately −70 mV.

This negative resting potential is maintained mainly by:

  • Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in)

  • High resting permeability to K⁺ through leak channels

The other options are incorrect because:

  • −65 mV – Close to threshold potential, not typical RMP.

  • −80 mV – More negative than nerve RMP; closer to some muscle cells.

  • −90 mV – Typical resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle fibres and ventricular cardiac myocytes.

High-yield points:

Cell type Resting membrane potential
Neuron −70 mV
Skeletal muscle −90 mV
Ventricular cardiac muscle −90 mV

Exam pearl:
Nerve fibre RMP = −70 mV.

Physiology-01.question: ১৭) Example of positive feedback mechanism except-
Physiology-01.option4: Insulin secretion in response to high blood glucose.
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is control of blood pressure because it is an example of a negative feedback mechanism, not positive feedback.

In negative feedback, the response opposes the initial change to maintain homeostasis.

Example:

  • ↑ Blood pressure → baroreceptors activated → ↓ sympathetic activity → heart rate and BP decrease

The other options are examples of positive feedback mechanisms:

  • Generation of nerve signals – Action potential involves positive feedback:

    • Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx → further depolarization → more Na⁺ channel opening

  • LH surge – Oestrogen from the mature follicle stimulates more LH release → ovulation.

  • Insulin secretion in response to high blood glucose – Increased glucose stimulates insulin release, which promotes glucose uptake and further regulates the response (often described as a positive feedback element in some physiology contexts).

High-yield points:

Positive feedback examples:

  • LH surge before ovulation

  • Action potential generation

  • Childbirth (oxytocin → uterine contraction)

Negative feedback examples:

  • Blood pressure regulation

  • Blood glucose regulation

  • Thyroid hormone regulation

Exam pearl:
Blood pressure control = negative feedback mechanism.

Physiology-01.question: ১৮) In smooth muscle calcium released by the smooth ER initiates contraction by binding to what protein?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is calmodulin. In smooth muscle, contraction is initiated when intracellular Ca²⁺ binds to calmodulin.

Mechanism:

  1. Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

  2. Ca²⁺ binds to calmodulin

  3. Ca²⁺–calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK)

  4. MLCK phosphorylates myosin light chains

  5. Actin–myosin interaction → smooth muscle contraction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Actin – Contractile protein that interacts with myosin but does not bind calcium directly in smooth muscle.

  • Desmin – Intermediate filament protein involved in structural support.

  • Myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) – Activated by the Ca²⁺–calmodulin complex; it is the enzyme responsible for myosin phosphorylation, not the initial calcium-binding protein.

High-yield points:

Smooth muscle contraction:

Ca²⁺ → Calmodulin → MLCK → Myosin phosphorylation → Contraction

Skeletal muscle:
Ca²⁺ → Troponin C → Contraction

Exam pearl:
Smooth muscle calcium receptor = Calmodulin.

Physiology-01.question: ১৯) Pinocytosis is -
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is cell drinking. Pinocytosis is a type of endocytosis in which a cell engulfs extracellular fluid and dissolved substances through small vesicles.

  • Pinocytosis = "cell drinking"

  • Phagocytosis = "cell eating"

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cell eating – Refers to phagocytosis, where large particles (e.g., bacteria) are engulfed.

  • Cell lysis – Breakdown or destruction of a cell membrane.

  • Cell shrinking – Occurs in conditions like dehydration or apoptosis, not pinocytosis.

High-yield points:

Endocytosis types:

  • Phagocytosis → Cell eating → Large particles

  • Pinocytosis → Cell drinking → Fluids + small solutes

  • Receptor-mediated endocytosis → Specific molecules (e.g., LDL)

Exam pearl:
Pinocytosis = drinking of extracellular fluid by the cell.

Physiology-01.question: ২০) VC+RV=?
২১) Direct method of measurement of cardiac output
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Fick method. The Fick principle is considered a direct method of measuring cardiac output.

Formula:

Cardiac Output=Oxygen consumptionArterial O2−Venous O2Cardiac Output=Arterial O2​−Venous O2​Oxygen consumption​

It measures:

  • Oxygen uptake by the body

  • Arteriovenous oxygen difference

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Indicator method – An indirect method using dilution of an injected indicator (e.g., dye or thermodilution).

  • Dye dilution method – A type of indicator dilution method; indirect.

  • Doppler echocardiography – Non-invasive estimation of cardiac output, not a direct measurement.

High-yield points:

Methods of cardiac output measurement:

Method Type
Fick principle Direct method
Indicator dilution Indirect
Dye dilution Indirect
Thermodilution Indirect
Doppler echo Non-invasive estimation

Exam pearl:
Direct measurement of cardiac output = Fick method.

Physiology-01.question: ২২) CO2 stimuli affecting respiratory center
Physiology-01.option2: Via CSF and brain interstitial fluid H+ concentration
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is via CSF and brain interstitial fluid H⁺ concentration.

CO₂ is the most important regulator of respiration. It crosses the blood–brain barrier easily and reacts with water:

CO2+H2O→H2CO3→H++HCO3−CO2​+H2​O→H2​CO3​→H++HCO3−​

The increased H⁺ concentration in CSF stimulates central chemoreceptors in the medulla, increasing respiratory drive.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Via baroreceptor – Baroreceptors regulate blood pressure, not CO₂ response.

  • Via carotid and aortic bodies – Peripheral chemoreceptors mainly respond to low O₂, but also detect increased CO₂ and H⁺; however, the major CO₂-mediated respiratory stimulation is through central chemoreceptors.

  • None of above – Incorrect.

High-yield points:

Respiratory regulation:

  • Central chemoreceptors (medulla) → ↑ CO₂ via ↑ CSF H⁺ (main mechanism)

  • Peripheral chemoreceptors:

    • Carotid bodies

    • Aortic bodies

    • Respond mainly to ↓ PaO₂

Exam pearl:
CO₂ stimulates respiration mainly by increasing CSF H⁺ concentration.

Physiology-01.question: ২৩) Substances synthesized and used in the lungs
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is surfactant. Pulmonary surfactant is synthesized and used in the lungs to reduce surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse.

Source:

  • Produced by Type II alveolar pneumocytes

Functions:

  • ↓ Alveolar surface tension

  • Prevents atelectasis

  • Improves lung compliance

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Prostaglandins – Can be synthesized in lungs but are not a major substance synthesized and used specifically for pulmonary function.

  • Histamine – Mainly released by mast cells; involved in allergic and inflammatory responses.

  • Kallikrein – A proteolytic enzyme involved in the kinin system, not a major pulmonary surfactant-related substance.

High-yield points:

Pulmonary surfactant:

  • Source → Type II pneumocytes

  • Main component → Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)

  • Appears around → 24 weeks gestation

  • Adequate by → 35 weeks gestation

Exam pearl:
Lung-synthesized functional substance = Surfactant.

Physiology-01.question: ২৪) The decrease in O2 affinity of hemoglobin when the pH of blood falls is called the
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Bohr effect. The Bohr effect describes the decrease in oxygen affinity of haemoglobin when blood pH falls (increased H⁺ concentration).

Mechanism:

  • ↓ pH (↑ H⁺) → haemoglobin releases O₂ more easily

  • Oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right

  • Improves oxygen delivery to tissues

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Haldane effect – Describes the effect of oxygenation of haemoglobin on CO₂ transport:

    • Oxygenated Hb carries less CO₂ and releases H⁺

  • Donnan effect – Relates to ion distribution across semipermeable membranes.

  • Channel effect – Not related to haemoglobin oxygen affinity.

High-yield points:

Bohr effect:

  • ↓ pH

  • ↑ CO₂

  • ↑ Temperature

  • ↑ 2,3-DPG
    → ↓ Hb affinity for O₂ → ↑ O₂ unloading

Exam pearl:
Low pH causing reduced Hb–O₂ affinity = Bohr effect.

Physiology-01.question: ২৫) Utilization of O2 by tissues is reduced in which form of hypoxia?
২৬) Maximum CO2 is transported as
Physiology-01.exp: Reference: Guyton 14th; P- 528

Physiology-01.question: ২৭) In smooth muscle acetylcholine bind with___ receptors.
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is muscarinic receptors. In smooth muscle, acetylcholine (ACh) mainly acts through muscarinic receptors.

Mechanism:

  • ACh binds to muscarinic receptors

  • Causes smooth muscle contraction (e.g., GI tract, bladder, bronchi)

  • Mediated mainly through M3 receptors via ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Nicotinic receptors – Found mainly in autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junction, not smooth muscle effector cells.

  • D1 receptors – Dopamine receptors involved mainly in renal vasodilation.

  • M2 receptors – Muscarinic receptors mainly found in the heart, causing ↓ heart rate; not the main smooth muscle receptor.

High-yield points:

Muscarinic receptor actions:

  • M1 → CNS, gastric glands

  • M2 → Heart (↓ HR)

  • M3 → Smooth muscle contraction + gland secretion

Exam pearl:
ACh on smooth muscle = Muscarinic (mainly M3) receptor.

Physiology-01.question: ২৮) “Powerhouses” of the cell-
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is mitochondria. Mitochondria are called the “powerhouses of the cell” because they produce most of the cell’s ATP (adenosine triphosphate) through oxidative phosphorylation.

Functions of mitochondria:

  • ATP production

  • Cellular respiration

  • Regulation of apoptosis

  • Calcium storage

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Nucleus – Contains DNA and controls cellular activities.

  • Ribosome – Site of protein synthesis.

  • Lysosomes – Responsible for intracellular digestion and breakdown of waste materials.

High-yield points:

Cell organelles:

  • Mitochondria → ATP production (“powerhouse”)

  • Nucleus → Control centre

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis

  • Lysosome → Suicidal bag of cell

Exam pearl:
Powerhouse of cell = Mitochondria.

Physiology-01.question: ২৯) Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) produce due to factor __ deficiency
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Factor IX deficiency. Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) is caused by a deficiency of clotting factor IX.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Factor XI deficiency → Haemophilia C

  • Factor VIII deficiency → Haemophilia A (classic haemophilia)

  • Factor XII deficiency → Causes prolonged APTT but usually no bleeding tendency

High-yield points:

Disease Factor deficiency
Haemophilia A Factor VIII
Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) Factor IX
Haemophilia C Factor XI

Exam pearl:
Christmas disease = Factor IX deficie

Physiology-01.question: ৩০) Blood clotting factor III
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Thromboplastin (Tissue factor). Coagulation factor III is also called tissue thromboplastin or tissue factor.

  • Factor III is released from damaged tissues.

  • It initiates the extrinsic coagulation pathway by activating Factor VII.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fibrinogen → Factor I

  • Prothrombin → Factor II

  • Calcium → Factor IV

High-yield points:

Factor Name
Factor I Fibrinogen
Factor II Prothrombin
Factor III Tissue thromboplastin (Tissue factor)
Factor IV Calcium
Factor VIII Anti-haemophilic factor
Factor IX Christmas factor

Exam pearl:
Factor III = Tissue thromboplastin = initiates extrinsic pathway.

Physiology-01.question: ৩১) Local factors produce vasoconstriction-
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is decreased local temperature. Local factors affecting blood vessels can cause either vasodilation or vasoconstriction.

Cold temperature causes:

  • Activation of vascular smooth muscle

  • Vasoconstriction

  • Reduced blood flow to conserve heat

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Increased CO₂ – Causes vasodilation (especially in tissues) to increase blood flow.

  • Decreased O₂ – Usually causes vasodilation in systemic tissues to improve oxygen delivery.

  • Decreased local pH – Causes vasodilation due to increased metabolic activity and need for oxygen.

High-yield points:

Local vasodilation factors:

  • ↑ CO₂

  • ↓ O₂

  • ↓ pH

  • ↑ Temperature

  • ↑ Adenosine, K⁺, lactate

Local vasoconstriction factor:

  • ↓ Temperature (cold exposure)

Exam pearl:
Cold → vasoconstriction; metabolic changes → vasodilation.

Physiology-01.question: ৩২) Cardiac output decreases in
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is standing from a lying position. When a person suddenly stands up, gravity causes pooling of blood in the lower limbs, leading to:

  • ↓ Venous return (↓ preload)

  • ↓ Stroke volume

  • ↓ Cardiac output (transiently)

The body compensates through baroreceptor reflex activation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Anxiety → ↑ sympathetic activity → ↑ heart rate and contractility → increased cardiac output

  • Eating → Increased metabolic activity and splanchnic blood flow → generally increases cardiac output

  • High environmental temperature → Skin vasodilation → increased cardiac output to maintain heat loss

High-yield points:

Factors increasing cardiac output:

  • Exercise

  • Anxiety

  • Eating

  • Pregnancy

  • Fever

Factors decreasing cardiac output:

  • Sudden standing (orthostatic change)

  • Reduced venous return

  • Severe haemorrhage

Exam pearl:
Standing suddenly → ↓ venous return → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ cardiac output.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৩) Factors that shift 02-Hb dissociation curve to left
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is increased pH. An increase in blood pH causes the O₂–haemoglobin dissociation curve to shift to the left, meaning haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen and releases less oxygen to tissues.

The other options cause a right shift:

  • Increased CO₂ → ↓ Hb affinity for O₂ (Bohr effect) → right shift

  • Increased temperature → ↓ Hb affinity for O₂ → right shift

  • Increased BPG (2,3-BPG) → ↓ Hb affinity for O₂ → right shift

High-yield points:

Left shift (↑ O₂ affinity):

  • ↑ pH (alkalosis)

  • ↓ CO₂

  • ↓ Temperature

  • ↓ 2,3-BPG

  • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)

Right shift (↑ O₂ unloading):

  • ↓ pH

  • ↑ CO₂

  • ↑ Temperature

  • ↑ 2,3-BPG

Exam pearl:
Alkalosis → left shift → oxygen binds more tightly to haemoglobin.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৪) BP on arm is measured over
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is brachial artery. Blood pressure is routinely measured over the brachial artery in the upper arm using a sphygmomanometer.

Method:

  • Cuff is placed around the upper arm

  • Stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery

  • Korotkoff sounds are used to determine systolic and diastolic pressure

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Radial artery – Used for pulse palpation, not standard BP measurement.

  • Ulnar artery – Not used for routine BP measurement.

  • Axillary artery – A proximal artery, not the standard auscultation site.

High-yield points:

Blood pressure measurement:

  • Cuff → upper arm

  • Artery assessed → Brachial artery

  • Sounds heard → Korotkoff sounds

Exam pearl:
Sphygmomanometer BP measurement = brachial artery.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৫) Can be measured by spirometry
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Vital capacity (VC). Spirometry measures lung volumes that involve air movement in and out of the lungs, including:

  • Vital capacity (VC)

  • Tidal volume (TV)

  • Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV)

  • Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Residual volume (RV) – Cannot be measured by simple spirometry because it is the air remaining after maximal expiration.

  • Functional residual capacity (FRC) – Cannot be measured by spirometry (requires gas dilution or body plethysmography).

  • Total lung capacity (TLC) – Cannot be measured by spirometry because it includes RV.

High-yield points:

Measured by spirometry:

  • TV

  • IRV

  • ERV

  • VC

Not measured by spirometry:

  • RV

  • FRC

  • TLC

Formula:

  • VC = IRV + TV + ERV

  • TLC = VC + RV

Exam pearl:
Spirometry measures vital capacity but not any volume containing residual volume.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৬) Primary expiratory muscle
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is internal intercostal muscles. During forced expiration, the internal intercostal muscles contract and pull the ribs downward and inward, helping to reduce thoracic volume and expel air.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Diaphragm – The primary muscle of inspiration; relaxation of the diaphragm contributes to quiet expiration.

  • Sternocleidomastoid – An accessory muscle of inspiration (especially during respiratory distress).

  • External intercostal muscles – Assist in inspiration by elevating the ribs.

High-yield points:

Respiratory muscles:

Inspiration:

  • Primary → Diaphragm

  • External intercostals

  • Accessory → SCM, scalenes

Forced expiration:

  • Internal intercostals

  • Abdominal muscles

Exam pearl:
Primary expiratory muscle = Internal intercostal muscle.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৭) The organelles playing an important role in intracellular digestion of the phagocytosed particles are-
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is lysosome. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest phagocytosed particles after they fuse with phagosomes to form phagolysosomes.

Mechanism:

  • Phagocytosis → Phagosome formation

  • Phagosome + Lysosome → Phagolysosome

  • Enzymes digest bacteria and cellular debris

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Mitochondria – Produce ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.

  • Ribosome – Responsible for protein synthesis.

  • Peroxisome – Involved in oxidation reactions and breakdown of fatty acids; contains catalase.

High-yield points:

Cell organelles:

  • Lysosome → Intracellular digestion (“suicidal bag”)

  • Mitochondria → ATP production

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis

  • Peroxisome → Detoxification + fatty acid oxidation

Exam pearl:
Phagocytosed particle digestion = Lysosome.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৮) Which organelle sorts and packages proteins within a cell?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Golgi apparatus. The Golgi apparatus is responsible for modifying, sorting, packaging, and transporting proteins received from the endoplasmic reticulum.

Functions:

  • Protein modification (e.g., glycosylation)

  • Sorting proteins to their destinations

  • Packaging into secretory vesicles

The other options are incorrect because:

  • SER (Smooth endoplasmic reticulum) – Synthesizes lipids, detoxifies drugs, and stores calcium; not mainly involved in protein sorting.

  • Lysosome – Performs intracellular digestion.

  • Mitochondria – Produces ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.

High-yield points:

Protein pathway:

Ribosome → Rough ER → Golgi apparatus → Secretory vesicles / Lysosomes / Cell membrane

Exam pearl:
Protein sorting and packaging = Golgi apparatus.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৯) Which cell is a respiratory macrophage?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is dust cells. Dust cells are the alveolar macrophages of the respiratory system.

Functions:

  • Phagocytose inhaled dust particles, bacteria, and debris

  • Protect alveoli from infection and particulate matter

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Kupffer cells – Macrophages present in the liver sinusoids.

  • Histiocytes – Tissue macrophages found in connective tissues.

  • Langerhans cells – Antigen-presenting dendritic cells found mainly in the skin and mucosa.

High-yield points:

Specialized macrophages:

Location Macrophage
Lung alveoli Dust cells
Liver Kupffer cells
Connective tissue Histiocytes
Skin epidermis Langerhans cells

Exam pearl:
Respiratory macrophage = Dust cell (alveolar macrophage).

Physiology-01.question: ৪০) Ventricular depolarisation in ECG is represented by
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is QRS complex. The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation on the ECG.

ECG components:

  • P wave → Atrial depolarisation

  • QRS complex → Ventricular depolarisation

  • T wave → Ventricular repolarisation

  • ST segment → Period when ventricles are fully depolarised (early ventricular systole)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • P wave – Represents electrical activation of the atria.

  • T wave – Represents ventricular repolarisation.

  • ST segment – Represents the plateau phase after ventricular depolarisation, not the depolarisation itself.

High-yield ECG points:

ECG component Represents
P wave Atrial depolarisation
PR interval AV conduction time
QRS complex Ventricular depolarisation
T wave Ventricular repolarisation

Exam pearl:
QRS = ventricular depolarisation.

Physiology-01.question: ৪১) The most important components of surfactant
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC). DPPC is the major and most important phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant.

Functions:

  • Reduces alveolar surface tension

  • Prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis)

  • Improves lung compliance

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Surfactant apoproteins – Important for surfactant function and immune defense (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D), but they are not the major component.

  • Calcium ions – Help stabilize surfactant films but are not the main constituent.

  • Cholesterol – Present in surfactant but not the principal component.

High-yield points:

Pulmonary surfactant composition:

  • DPPC (lecithin) → Major component (~70–80% of phospholipids)

  • Phosphatidylglycerol

  • Surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D)

  • Cholesterol

Exam pearl:
Most important surfactant component = Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC).

Physiology-01.question: ৪২) Which play an important role in the defense mechanism of the body against the parasites?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is eosinophils. Eosinophils play an important role in the body's defense against parasitic infections, especially helminths (worms).

Mechanism:

  • Eosinophils attach to parasites through IgE-mediated mechanisms.

  • Release major basic protein and other toxic granules that damage parasites.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutrophils – Mainly defend against bacterial infections through phagocytosis.

  • Basophils – Involved in allergic reactions and release histamine; also participate in IgE responses.

  • Monocytes – Become macrophages and perform phagocytosis of microbes and debris.

High-yield points:

Cell Main function
Eosinophils Parasite defense + allergy
Neutrophils Bacterial infection
Basophils Histamine release, allergy
Monocytes/macrophages Phagocytosis

Exam pearl:
Helminth infection → eosinophilia → eosinophils.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৩) Agglutinogens are present in
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is RBC membrane. Agglutinogens are antigens present on the surface of red blood cells that determine the ABO blood group.

Examples:

  • A antigen → Blood group A

  • B antigen → Blood group B

  • A + B antigens → Blood group AB

  • No A/B antigen → Blood group O

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Platelet membrane – Contains platelet antigens but not ABO agglutinogens responsible for blood grouping.

  • Serum – Contains agglutinins (antibodies), not agglutinogens.

  • WBC membrane – Does not contain ABO agglutinogens used for routine blood grouping.

High-yield points:

ABO system:

  • Agglutinogen = Antigen → RBC surface

  • Agglutinin = Antibody → Plasma/serum

Blood group RBC antigen Plasma antibody
A A Anti-B
B B Anti-A
AB A + B None
O None Anti-A + Anti-B

Exam pearl:
Agglutinogens are present on RBC membrane.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৪) Propagation of action potential through
৪৫) Which enzyme is required in fibrinolysis?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is plasminogen. In fibrinolysis, plasminogen is converted into plasmin, the active enzyme responsible for breaking down fibrin clots.

Mechanism:

  • Plasminogen → Plasmin (activated by tissue plasminogen activator, tPA)

  • Plasmin → degrades fibrin → fibrin degradation products (including D-dimer)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Caspases – Enzymes involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death).

  • Thrombin – Promotes coagulation by converting fibrinogen to fibrin; opposite function.

  • Antithrombin III – Inhibits clotting factors (especially thrombin and factor Xa); an anticoagulant, not a fibrinolytic enzyme.

High-yield points:

Fibrinolysis pathway:

Plasminogen → (tPA) → Plasmin → Fibrin breakdown

Exam pearl:
Key enzyme of fibrinolysis = Plasmin (derived from plasminogen).

Physiology-01.question: ৪৬) Key reaction of coagulation in each pathway is
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is activation of Factor X. The key reaction common to both intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways is the activation of Factor X (Xa), which marks the start of the common pathway.

Pathway:

  • Intrinsic pathway: XII → XI → IX + VIII → X

  • Extrinsic pathway: VII + Tissue factor → X

  • Common pathway: X → Xa → II (prothrombin) → thrombin → I (fibrinogen) → fibrin

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Activation of Factor VII – Initiates the extrinsic pathway only.

  • Activation of Factor II – Occurs later in the common pathway; thrombin formation.

  • Activation of Factor XII – Initiates the intrinsic pathway only.

High-yield points:

Key steps of coagulation:

  • Intrinsic + Extrinsic pathways converge at Factor X activation

  • Factor Xa converts prothrombin (II) → thrombin

  • Thrombin converts fibrinogen (I) → fibrin

Exam pearl:
Common key reaction of coagulation = Factor X activation.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৭) Which volume remains in the lungs after a tidal volume (TV) is expired?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Functional residual capacity (FRC).

After a normal tidal volume (TV) expiration, the volume of air remaining in the lungs is the functional residual capacity.

FRC = ERV + RVFRC = ERV + RV

It represents:

  • Air left in lungs after normal expiration

  • Maintains continuous gas exchange between breaths

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Vital capacity (VC) – Maximum amount of air exhaled after maximal inspiration.

  • Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) – Extra air that can be forcefully expired after a normal expiration.

  • Residual volume (RV) – Air remaining after maximal forced expiration, not after tidal expiration.

High-yield points:

Event Remaining volume
After normal expiration (TV expired) FRC
After maximal expiration RV
Maximum expired after maximal inspiration VC

Exam pearl:
End of normal tidal expiration = Functional residual capacity (FRC).

Physiology-01.question: ৪৮) Following which is the main muscle of inspiration -?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is diaphragm. The diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration, responsible for about 75% of the increase in thoracic volume during quiet breathing.

Mechanism:

  • Diaphragm contracts → moves downward

  • Thoracic cavity volume increases

  • Intrapulmonary pressure falls

  • Air enters the lungs

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pectoralis major – Accessory muscle of forced inspiration.

  • Latissimus dorsi – Assists in forced respiratory movements but is not the primary inspiratory muscle.

  • Transverse thoracis – Assists expiration by depressing ribs.

High-yield points:

Muscles of respiration:

Quiet inspiration:

  • Diaphragm (main)

  • External intercostal muscles

Forced inspiration:

  • Sternocleidomastoid

  • Scalenes

  • Pectoral muscles

Forced expiration:

  • Internal intercostals

  • Abdominal muscles

Exam pearl:
Main muscle of inspiration = Diaphragm.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৯) Which of the following is responsible for the movement of O2 from the alveoli into the blood in the pulmonary capillaries?
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is passive diffusion. Oxygen moves from the alveoli into pulmonary capillary blood by simple passive diffusion across the alveolar–capillary membrane.

Mechanism:

  • Oxygen moves from an area of higher partial pressure in alveoli (↑PO₂)

  • To an area of lower partial pressure in pulmonary capillary blood (↓PO₂)

  • No energy or carrier protein is required

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Active transport – Requires energy (ATP) and carrier proteins; not involved in O₂ exchange.

  • Secondary active transport – Uses an ion gradient; not involved in gas exchange.

  • Facilitated diffusion – Requires carrier proteins; oxygen crosses membranes directly due to its lipid solubility.

High-yield points:

Alveolar gas exchange:

  • O₂ → Passive diffusion

  • CO₂ → Passive diffusion

  • Driven by partial pressure gradients

Exam pearl:
Oxygen transfer from alveoli to blood = simple passive diffusion.

Physiology-01.question: ৫০) Airway resistance
Physiology-01.option1: is increased if the lungs are removed and inflated with saline.
Physiology-01.option2: does not affect the work of breathing.
Physiology-01.option4: is increased following bronchial smooth muscle contraction.
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is airway resistance increases following bronchial smooth muscle contraction.

Mechanism:

  • Bronchial smooth muscle contraction → airway diameter decreases

  • Resistance to airflow increases

  • Seen in conditions like asthma

According to Poiseuille’s law:

Resistance∝1r4Resistance∝r41​

A small reduction in airway radius causes a large increase in resistance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Lungs removed and inflated with saline → Airway resistance is decreased, because saline removes the air–tissue interface and reduces elastic recoil effects.

  • Does not affect the work of breathing → Incorrect. Increased airway resistance increases the work of breathing.

  • Increased in paraplegic patients → Incorrect. Paraplegia mainly affects respiratory muscle function and reduces ventilation; airway resistance is not primarily increased.

High-yield points:

Factors increasing airway resistance:

  • Bronchoconstriction (asthma)

  • Mucus secretion

  • Airway obstruction

  • Reduced airway radius

Exam pearl:
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction → ↓ airway radius → ↑ airway resistance.
